t: The 4 Cornerstones Of Smart Classroom Management nagement/
q: These principles, or cornerstones, form the heart of what we believe to be the solution to the scores of behavior-related challenges facing teachers today.
Any method or strategy that causes friction with students will always make classroom management more difficult.
It creates resentment and animosity. It causes students to secretly dislike you and misbehave behind your back.
All students—difficult, shy, and confident alike—are drawn to teachers who exude a calm, friendly demeanor.
It is the love of school that is the ultimate reward, the ultimate intrinsic motivator, and the ultimate antidote to unwanted behavior.
Allowing your classroom management plan to be the lone source of accountability removes the need to rely on hurtful and less effective methods of managing behavior.
We offer one unified approach, where every strategy works together harmoniously to craft the optimum teaching and learning environment.

t: For Noncognitive Skill Development, Start with Growth Mindset — Here’s How
q: Growth mindset allows kids to see challenges as opportunities to grow rather than daunting judgments on who they are.
Few would argue that calling a kid stupid is a bad idea. What many find surprising, though, is that the opposite — calling a kid smart — is bad, too.

In the study, Dweck took two groups of elementary students; one group was praised for being smart, the other was praised for working hard. After this, both groups were given the chance to take a challenging assessment. The “smart” group was hesitant to take the assessment, while the “hard working” group was open to trying.

Essentially, Dweck found that praising kids in a fixed manner — in this case, that their achievement was due to the fixed state of “being smart” — retards both their motivation to engage with challenges and with the actual performance on assessments, whereas praising kids in a growth manner — in other words, attributing their success to hard work — propels their growth in the long term.

In other words, if you were to give my students Dweck’s mindset questionnaire, virtually all of them would test for growth mindset. Yet I still have a fraction of students who do not put in the necessary work to put themselves on the road to college and career readiness.

The way we frame activities [is influential in developing dynamic-learning frame in students]. For example, introducing an activity by saying ‘Let’s see who’s the best (or quickest) at doing these problems’ is very different from ‘Let’s see which of these problems is the most interesting.’ These will lead children to different understandings of what they are doing, focus their attention on different information, and turn their energies toward different goals.
x: Stories are the stickiest vehicle for mindset, so teachers should build a go-to repertoire of hard-work stories rather than rely on slogans.

t: Why You Should Let Poorly Followed Routines Play Out s-play-out/
q: Upon noticing a class routine going off the rails, they immediately jump in to try and correct it.
It’s far better to take a step back and let the routine play out.
The only way to fix a sloppy routine so that it doesn’t happen again is to know precisely what went wrong.

When students know they’re being watched intently, especially by a teacher who faithfully holds them accountable for previously learned expectations, they develop the ability to recognize and correct their own mistakes.
When you jump in right away, on the other hand, they’re likely to become defensive, argumentative, and annoyed by your interruption.
Handling misbehavior with patience and composure, on the other hand, will calm and settle your students and refocus them on the task at hand.
Only then will your students begin looking inward at themselves and their responsibilities.
x: Linsin advises against the common instinct to jump in and correct a sloppily executed routine as soon as it starts going wrong.
He gives four reasons to instead observe from a distance and let it play out.
Letting a sloppy routine play out lets the teacher accurately diagnose whether it's a behavior problem or a misunderstanding.
Watching without intervening gives students a chance to self-correct and recognize mistakes on their own.

t: Literacy Educators: Let’s Get Serious about Noncognitive Skills
q: However, here’s the claim I’ll spend this post supporting (I've pawed around in the dark at it elsewhere, but that was quite a few months ago, and I've done more thinking in the interim): if you aim at the Common Core's goals (which are cognitive) and nothing else, you and/or a large amount of your students will begin to hate you and/or their life. A vague sense of frustration will live in your classroom, and you won't be able to put your finger on it.

Noncognitive skills are those things that aren't measured on traditional intelligence metrics (e.g., IQ) but are nonetheless being shown in study after study to significantly predict whether or not you’ll be successful. By calling them skills, I'm saying that, just like dribbling a soccer ball or writing your name or factoring an equation or reading closely, noncognitive skills can be intentionally taught and intentionally practiced and intentionally mastered.

But I would also argue that most teachers lack a systematic, simplified list of what noncognitive skills matter for their students' long-term flourishing. As a result, their attempts to instill noncognitive skills in their students are inefficient at least and, unfortunately, often largely ineffective.

But I would argue that anything that's got a shot of really having an impact in education should be complex enough to explore creatively for years and yet simplifiable enough to understand, in some fashion, in as little as an hour. We need simplified literacy instruction frameworks like the non-freaked out approach if we're to see kids getting more and better literacy instruction throughout their school day in all their classes.

The problem with the claim, though, is that I think we need relationships and systems to maximize the impact of our teaching, especially if great teaching is going to spread as far as it can go. Professions have frameworks and systems for describing best practices, and ours is a profession.

To get us back to our topic, the key, I think, lies in viewing systematic noncognitive skill lists as descriptive rather than prescriptive. Jim's list is a description of what proficient students can do. The KIPP list is a description of a set of habits that increase the likelihood of positive life outcomes.

But here's the gist — the literacy instruction conversation needs to include the noncognitive skill conversation, and we need to move forward with agreed upon language for referring to what skills matter most so that we, as a community of professionals, can get to the much more exciting work of exploring how in the world we get kids developing these highly predictive, literacy-enhancing skills.
x: Stuart's core claim: literacy instruction aimed solely at the Common Core's cognitive goals will leave a vague frustration in the classroom unless noncognitive skills are taught strategically.

Drawing on Paul Tough's How Children Succeed and James Heckman's work, he defines noncognitive skills as learnable habits, such as grit and self-control, that predict success but are not measured by intelligence metrics.
His diagnosis is that most teachers care about these skills but lack a systematic, simplified list of which ones matter, largely because high-stakes testing rewards only cognitive gains.

He traces teachers' lack of systematic noncognitive lists to decades of test-driven emphasis on cognitive skills, where there is no test for grit or self-control.
He closes by calling for a shared professional language so that noncognitive skills enter the literacy conversation explicitly.

t: How A Simple Change In Thinking Can Improve Behavior ve-behavior/
q: One of the reasons difficult students misbehave is because their teacher expects that they will.
To combat this phenomenon, you must do the opposite. You must assume henceforth that your most challenging students will, of their own accord, behave . . . perfectly.
That isn’t to say that you’ll become lax in your supervision, ignore their misbehavior, or in any way become less consistent holding them accountable.
This simple change in thinking—in how you choose to see them—effectively removes an infinite number of verbal and non-verbal signals that reinforce their poor behavior.
It upends their attitude toward you, transforming them from someone who firmly believes that you’re out to get them . . . into your biggest fan.
They’ll see in your eyes a reflection of themselves they may not at first recognize, but who deep down they’ve always wanted to be.
x: Teacher expectations of misbehavior function as a self-fulfilling prophecy for difficult students.
The prescribed fix is a deliberate internal reframe: assume difficult students will behave well, without lowering actual supervision or accountability standards.
He explains that this shift removes the accumulated negative signals—tone, body language, anticipatory tension—that reinforce a student's poor self-image and defiance.
This reframe removes subtle verbal and nonverbal cues that unintentionally signal distrust or resentment.
The shift can transform a student's attitude from believing the teacher is 'out to get them' to seeing the teacher as an ally.

t: 4 Jedi Mind Tricks for Avoiding Burnout
q: So here’s what few teacher books will tell you — great teaching is only possible when your heart is in it, and yet there are so many factors seemingly bent on removing our hearts completely. Back when I started this blog, I considered standards one more group of things that were out to “get” us teachers, to rip out the heart of our profession.

As a new teacher, I used to look down on older, burnt out teachers until I realized that none of them, years ago with newly minted teaching certificates in their hands, dreamed of one day becoming burnt out gripemasters.
When your job performance is linked, inside your head and heart, to your worth as a person, success will affect you like a narcotic. You will become proud; you will think you’re super-amazing.

I went from the guy who fails mopingly to the guy who fails excitedly because of the lessons I was learning. It turned my worst days into some of my most productive; days in which my greatest weaknesses were laid bare like those nightmares where you realized you’re not wearing pants became days in which my strength as a teacher grew the most.

My goal is not to be the messiah of my students — it is to impact them. For the rest of the year, I was able to use my increased influence with Belle to help her grow in her literacy skills, simply because I made the right call in the tough situation.

I’m not saying be a jerk to kids — I am saying you’ve got to have higher goals than to simply have them love you. Interestingly enough, since I’ve started to embrace this, I’ve found that I am more liked by students, not less.
x: The piece is a career-sustainability argument for the profession side of teaching.
Dave Stuart Jr. argues that lasting impact in teaching depends on tending the teacher's own heart and mind, which he likens to a garden that decays if left on autopilot.
Tying identity to job performance wrecks teachers in both directions: success breeds pride and dependence, failure breeds shame and cynicism.
Reframing each classroom failure as someone getting smarter (the teacher) turned his worst student-teaching days into his most productive ones.
Teachers should visibly pursue the character strengths they hope students will grow, treating hard seasons as a furnace for their own character.

t: Why You Must Remind Students Of Their Purpose https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/07/05/why-you-must-remind-students-of-their-purpose/
q: If not reminded, and reminded often, your students will naturally slip into believing that school is just something they’re supposed to do.
This attitude can cause students to take their education for granted, to see it as a grind, as something they’re forced to do rather than what it is.
Doing anything begrudgingly, anything with the specter of having to do it hanging over your head, can be a dangerous thing.
It is the ‘why’ of school, after all, that cracks ajar the gates of learning.
You tell them. You tell them every day why they’re there, why what they’re doing is important, and why what you have to offer them is a most precious gift.
Coming from someone your students like and admire, and delivered with passion, this simple message—which will vary in depth depending on grade level—can be powerful and deeply impressionable.
x: Without regular reminders of purpose, students drift into seeing school as an obligation rather than an opportunity.
